I've had to go through hell these last two years. Constantly moving, living out of a suitcase, unrelenting time crunch, infrequent gym access. It's been a journey that's forced me to reassess what I think fitness even *is* and what I want out of it personally. I went in as a pure barbells guy and came out on the other side as a fanatical BWF and improvised gear type.

*I keep referring to my isometric trainer. It's not exactly what you see in the video, but this is a great demo of the principle and use:* https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y9G0B4Fy1j0

Here's my day to day routine.

> Day 1: Push

1. Superset: handstand push ups, wall dips, 3-5 sets to failure each. Usually when handstand push ups get below 5 reps I will switch to pike push ups instead for volume's sake.

2. Decline push ups, 3-5 sets to failure.

3. Front & side planks. I do these by moving my hips up and down in a slow controlled fashion so I burn faster, because pure isometrics are boring and time consuming. I usually do 3-5 sets of 20+, alternating front and side planks.

4. Reverse curls on the isometric trainer shown in my other thread.

5. Self resisted reverse wrist curls. Lay your hand over your thigh like you're going to do reverse wrist curls, but instead of picking up a weight, just push down on the back of your hand using your other hand. Work through the full movement. I do 3-5x20.

6. Neck work. I train the front of my neck by laying on my back, keeping my head off the ground, and slowly turning my head side to side as if saying "no." Again, 3-5x20+.

7. Optional: wrist radial deviation and pronation. I work this with self resistance holding a stick, metal bar, tool or anything else that can provide a lever. Push on it with one hand while working through the range of motion. I do it for 3-5x20.

> Day 2: Pull

1. Pull ups. No pull up bar, I think owning a pull up bar is bullshit, I do them on rafters or whatever else is available. If nothing is available for conventional pull ups I do "cat hang" pull ups on a wall. I do at least 30 total in whatever sets it takes.

2. Rows. Equipment is either a walkway hand rail, the underside of a table or a broom across two chairs (or anything else I can find that does the job). I do them underhand for bicep activation, explosive on the way up and slow on the way down, for sets of 10 until I'm trashed. I don't know why I do it this way, I just do.

3. Shrugs with the best available. Priority: iso trainer > inverting myself on a bar/rings and shrugging myself up > handstand shrugs against a wall. With the iso trainer I find that any upper body move burns more and gets a more effective workout if I "pump" my legs up and down while resisting with my upper body, shrugs are no different.

4. Rear neck training. I used to do bridges but the volume/frequency started giving me headaches that I can't afford, so now I get down on elbows and knees and "headbang" my head up and down slow and controlled until the back of my neck burns really badly. Usually I do 50+, 20 and 20.

5. Grip. My sole grip work these days is to wad up a small towel and alternately squeeze it with each hand as hard as I can until my hands and forearms burn out. It's the same principle as rice bucket training, just cleaner and more portable. I like to turn the towel in my lap every time I release it, so that the shape I have to grab keeps changing. I can reliably hold on to double bodyweight in a double overhand grip when I have access to barbells, so I take that as evidence that it works.

6. Radial deviation training. As above, use any item that works as a lever and self resist it. I don't bother training supination because of all the work my biceps get.

> Day 3: Legs

1. Isometric deadlift on my training device. If for some reason this is not available, there are simple techniques for hooking yourself onto many things for back extensions. A good and versatile technique is seen here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nlWNPMshDoo

2. Horse stance training & lunge stance training. I am pleased to see other people here who know about this stuff. Again, I lost patience for pure isometrics so I slowly raise and lower my hips for reps. I alternate horse stance with lunge stance on both sides, doing sets of 20 until I'm really tired and wobbly.

3. Front and side kicks. These really help my hip flexors/abductors and overall explosiveness and athleticism. I usually do 20 front kicks each side, 20 side kicks each side, repeat until really tired.

4. Optional step ups. Take to fatigue 3-5x.

5. Footwork drills for calves. I basically jump rope without the rope, and mix sprinting, faking, braking and cornering drills in randomly until my calves burn like mad. Take to fatigue 3-5x.

6. Optional hamstring drill for grappling: Take a kneeling position, put your hands on your forehead, now bend down until your elbows touch your knees. Get back up again. Repeat in sets of 20 until you burn. This helps me in the top position.

Usually I work out every other day.
